kcet|Chemistry|2014|26||0|0:
The target is acetophenone, C₆H₅COCH₃. Check which starting material reaches it in one easy step.
(2) Benzene — Friedel–Crafts acylation with CH₃COCl and anhydrous AlCl₃ gives acetophenone
directly ✓ This is the standard preparation.
(3) 1-Phenylethanol, C₆H₅CH(OH)CH₃ — a secondary alcohol; mild oxidation gives the ketone ✓
(4) Phenylacetylene, C₆H₅C≡CH — hydration with H₂SO₄/HgSO₄ adds water by Markovnikov's rule,
putting the OH on the substituted carbon, and the enol tautomerises to acetophenone ✓
(1) Toluene, C₆H₅CH₃ — there is no easy route. Oxidising the methyl group does not stop at a
ketone; it goes straight through to benzoic acid, C₆H₅COOH, because the carbon is attached to
the ring and oxidation of a benzylic CH₃ always ends at the carboxyl stage.
∴ acetophenone cannot be prepared easily from toluene.

kcet|Chemistry|2014|30||0|0.s:
Sodium methoxide is a nucleophile, so this is nucleophilic aromatic substitution, and the rate
depends on how well the negatively charged intermediate is stabilised.
A nitro group stabilises that intermediate strongly — but only from the **ortho or para**
position, because only those put the negative charge where the nitro group can delocalise it.
From the meta position it cannot help at all.
Now rank them:
(4) Chlorobenzene — no nitro group, essentially unreactive.
(2) The nitro group is meta to Cl, so no resonance stabilisation: barely better than chlorobenzene.
(1) One nitro group para to Cl: activated.
(3) Two nitro groups, one ortho and one para to the chlorine. Both are in positions that can
delocalise the charge, so the intermediate is stabilised twice over.
2,4-Dinitrochlorobenzene reacts far faster than the mononitro compound.
∴ compound (3).

kcet|Chemistry|2014|32||0|0.s:
Get the solubility from the conductivity, then square it for Ksp.
Molar conductivity relates the two:
Λm = κ/c  ⇒  c = κ/Λ°m
For a sparingly soluble salt the saturated solution is so dilute that Λm ≈ Λ°m.
c = 1.85 × 10⁻⁵ / (140 × 10⁻⁴)
c = 1.85 × 10⁻⁵ / 1.40 × 10⁻²
c = 1.321 × 10⁻³ mol m⁻³
The units here are SI, so convert to mol L⁻¹: 1 mol m⁻³ = 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹
c = 1.321 × 10⁻⁶ mol L⁻¹
AB dissociates one-to-one, so [A⁺] = [B⁻] = c:
Ksp = c² = (1.321 × 10⁻⁶)² = 1.74 × 10⁻¹²
∴ Ksp = 1.74 × 10⁻¹².

kcet|Chemistry|2014|33||0|0.s:
Find the false statement.
(2) True — a weak nucleophile cannot force a backside attack, and a protic solvent hydrogen
bonds to the leaving group and stabilises the carbocation, both of which favour SN1.
(3) True — a strong nucleophile drives the backside attack, and a polar aprotic solvent leaves
that nucleophile unencumbered, so SN2 is favoured.
(4) True — a Lewis acid such as Ag⁺ or AlCl₃ co-ordinates to the halogen and helps it leave,
speeding the ionisation step of SN1.
(1) False — rearrangement is a feature of **SN1**, not SN2. SN1 goes through a carbocation,
which can shift a hydride or methyl to become more stable, giving a rearranged product.
SN2 has no carbocation at all; it is one concerted step, so nothing can rearrange. The reaction
that actually competes with SN2 is elimination, E2.
∴ statement (1) is incorrect.

kcet|Chemistry|2014|34||0|0.s:
Butylated hydroxy toluene (BHT), with its close relative BHA, is added to fats, oils and
packaged foods to stop them going rancid.
Rancidity is a free radical chain oxidation of the unsaturated fats by atmospheric oxygen.
BHT is a hindered phenol: it donates the hydrogen of its –OH to a chain-carrying radical,
terminating the chain, and the phenoxy radical left behind is too stable and too sterically
hindered to continue it.
That makes it an **antioxidant**.
The other roles belong to different additives: flavouring agents such as esters, emulsifiers
such as lecithin, and colouring agents such as tartrazine.
∴ an antioxidant.

kcet|Chemistry|2014|35||0|0:
Terylene (Dacron) is made by condensing ethylene glycol with terephthalic acid, losing water
at each link:
n HOCH₂CH₂OH + n HOOC–C₆H₄–COOH ⇒ [–OCH₂CH₂OOC–C₆H₄–CO–]ₙ + 2n H₂O
So check each description.
(1) Polyester fibre ✓ — the repeating link is the ester group –COO–.
(2) Step growth polymer ✓ — monomers join in steps, any two chain ends can react, and a small
molecule (water) is eliminated at each step. That is the definition of condensation polymerisation.
(3) Copolymer ✓ — it is built from two different monomers.
(4) Chain growth polymer ✗ — chain growth means monomers add one at a time to an active
chain end, usually across a double bond, with nothing eliminated. Polythene and PVC are chain
growth; terylene is not.
∴ terylene is NOT a chain growth polymer.
kcet|Chemistry|2014|36||0|0:
Benzene + 3H₂ ⇒ cyclohexane, and the aromatic ring resists it.
(1) False — with one mole of each, hydrogen is the limiting reagent: 1 mol H₂ can make only
1/3 mol of cyclohexane, and it is all consumed. What is left over is 2/3 mol of **benzene**,
not hydrogen.
(2) False — cyclohexene has an ordinary isolated double bond and hydrogenates readily.
Benzene has 150 kJ mol⁻¹ of resonance energy that must be given up before the first addition,
so benzene is the *harder* of the two.
(4) False — hydrogenation is exothermic, about −208 kJ mol⁻¹ for benzene to cyclohexane.
(3) True — this follows from (2). Once the first addition breaks the aromatic system, the
cyclohexadiene formed has no resonance stabilisation left and is hydrogenated *faster* than
benzene itself. So the intermediates never accumulate and cannot be isolated easily.
∴ statement (3) is correct.

kcet|Chemistry|2014|39||0|0.s:
Check first whether the species are isoelectronic, because that makes the comparison simple.
Ca²⁺ : Z = 20, 20 − 2 = 18 electrons
K⁺  : Z = 19, 19 − 1 = 18 electrons
S²⁻ : Z = 16, 16 + 2 = 18 electrons
All three have 18 electrons, so the same number of shells and the same shielding.
For isoelectronic species, size is decided by nuclear charge alone: the more protons, the harder
the same 18 electrons are pulled in, and the smaller the ion.
Z = 20 > 19 > 16, so radius runs the other way:
Ca²⁺ < K⁺ < S²⁻
That is increasing order, which is what the question asks for.
The other options mix species that are not isoelectronic, so no single rule orders them.
∴ Ca²⁺ < K⁺ < S²⁻.

kcet|Chemistry|2014|40||0|0:
Bond length falls as bond order rises, so work out the C–O bond order in each.
CO — a triple bond, bond order 3. The shortest C–O bond there is, 113 pm.
CO₂ — O=C=O, two double bonds, bond order 2, about 116 pm.
HCO₃⁻ — one C–OH single bond and two oxygens sharing a double bond by resonance, so those
two have bond order 1.5, about 126 pm.
CO₃²⁻ — one double bond shared equally over three oxygens, bond order 4/3 = 1.33. The lowest
of the four, so the longest bond, about 129 pm.
Now put them in **decreasing** order of bond length, which is increasing order of bond order:
CO₃²⁻ > HCO₃⁻ > CO₂ > CO
∴ CO₃²⁻, HCO₃⁻, CO₂, CO.

kcet|Chemistry|2014|41||0|0.s:
Hydrolysis needs the water to attack a polarised or electron-deficient centre. Covalent
compounds of this kind are attacked readily; a simple ionic solid is not.
(2) CaC₂ + 2H₂O ⇒ Ca(OH)₂ + C₂H₂ — the carbide ion is a strong base and takes protons from
water, giving acetylene.
(3) P₄O₁₀ + 6H₂O ⇒ 4H₃PO₄ — a covalent acidic oxide, hydrolysed so eagerly that it is used as
a drying agent.
(4) Mg₃N₂ + 6H₂O ⇒ 3Mg(OH)₂ + 2NH₃ — the nitride ion is strongly basic and liberates ammonia.
(1) BaO₂ is an ionic peroxide of a large, strongly electropositive metal. It simply dissolves
as Ba²⁺ and O₂²⁻ without being broken down by water; H₂O₂ is obtained from it by treating it
with an **acid**, not with water alone.
∴ BaO₂ is not hydrolysed in water.

kcet|Chemistry|2014|44||0|0.s:
The iodoform test needs either a methyl ketone, CH₃–CO–, or an alcohol of the form
CH₃–CH(OH)–, which I₂/NaOH oxidises to that ketone first.
So look for a CH₃ attached directly to the carbon bearing the C=O or the OH.
(1) CH₃CHO — the methyl is next to the carbonyl ✓
(4) CH₃CH₂OH — written out, CH₃–CH(OH)–H has the required CH₃–CH(OH)– unit; it is oxidised
to ethanal and then gives iodoform ✓ (ethanol is the one primary alcohol that responds)
(3) CH₃–CH(OH)–CH₂–COOH — the second carbon carries both a methyl and the OH ✓
(2) CH₃CH₂CH₂OH — the carbon bearing the OH holds two hydrogens and an ethyl group, not a
methyl. Oxidation gives propanal and then propanoic acid, neither of which is a methyl ketone.
∴ propan-1-ol does not answer the iodoform test.
